blocks.prompt: 6. Show that the ratio of the sum of first \(n\) terms of a G.P. to the sum of terms from \((n + 1)\)th to \((2n)\)th term is \(\frac{1}{r^{n}}\), where \(r\) is the common ratio of G.P.
blocks.explanation:
A proof. The terms from the \((n+1)\)th to the \((2n)\)th are themselves a G.P. of \(n\) terms with the same ratio \(r\).
Plan: write both sums with the G.P. sum formula and divide (assume \(r \neq 1\) and \(r^{n} \neq 1\) so nothing is zero; for \(r = 1\) both sums are \(na_1\) and the ratio is \(1 = \frac{1}{1^{n}}\)).
steps:
Given: a G.P. \(a_1, a_1 r, a_1 r^{2}, \ldots\)
To prove: \(\dfrac{S_n}{a_{n+1} + \cdots + a_{2n}} = \dfrac{1}{r^{n}}\).
Method: Use \(S_n = \frac{a_1(1 - r^{n})}{1 - r}\) for both groups of terms.

Sum of the first \(n\) terms
\[S_n = \dfrac{a_1(1 - r^{n})}{1 - r}\]
Why: The standard G.P. sum formula.

The second group of terms
\[a_{n+1} = a_1 r^{n}\]
\[a_{n+1} + \cdots + a_{2n} = \dfrac{a_1 r^{n}(1 - r^{n})}{1 - r}\]
Why: From the \((n+1)\)th to the \((2n)\)th there are \(2n - n = n\) terms, a G.P. with first term \(a_1 r^{n}\) and ratio \(r\).

Divide
\[\dfrac{S_n}{a_{n+1} + \cdots + a_{2n}} = \dfrac{a_1(1 - r^{n})}{a_1 r^{n}(1 - r^{n})}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{r^{n}}\]
Why: The common bottom \(1 - r\) cancels, then \(a_1\) and \((1 - r^{n})\) cancel.

Check: with numbers
\[1, 2, 4, 8:\ \ n = 2,\ r = 2\]
\[\dfrac{1 + 2}{4 + 8} = \dfrac{3}{12} = \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2^{2}}\]
Why: The first two terms over the next two terms gives \(\frac{1}{r^{n}}\), as proved.
